Demand Generation Economics

The Commercial SystemPart 8

By lowob · 17 November 2026 · 9-minute read · Growth

In short: Demand generation should be managed on the cost of a qualified opportunity and the time it takes a won customer to pay that cost back, not on lead volume. Forrester's research finds fewer than 1% of leads convert to closed deals, so a programme optimised for leads is optimised for the wrong thing. Work backwards from a payback target and every channel gets a ceiling: the most it can spend to produce one qualified opportunity. The harder part is that buyers are, by 6sense's estimate, nearly 70% through their process before they speak to a seller, so the spend that creates demand is the spend that is hardest to measure.

Key points

  • The unit of demand is the qualified opportunity, not the lead; fewer than 1% of leads become closed deals.
  • CAC payback is customer acquisition cost divided by monthly revenue per account after gross margin; it links demand spend to cash.
  • A payback target, worked backwards, sets a maximum cost per qualified opportunity for every channel.
  • Payback alone misleads: firms with short payback and high retention grew about seven times faster than those with neither in one 2025 benchmark.
  • Capture spend harvests demand that already exists and always looks cheap; creation spend builds it and always looks expensive.

Part 7 set out the commercial measures a board will trust. CAC payback was one of them. This part opens it up, because the number a board sees at the end of a quarter is the product of dozens of smaller spending decisions made by the marketing team during it. If those decisions are made on lead volume or cost per click, the payback figure arrives as a surprise. If they are made on the same chain the board uses, it does not.

Lead volume is the wrong unit

Most marketing teams still report leads, and many are paid on them. The problem is that the lead is a poor proxy for what the business buys. Forrester's analysis, published in November 2023, found fewer than 1% of leads convert to closed deals, and that multiple leads typically feed a single opportunity. The same work found 28% of B2B buyers purchase in groups of four to nine people and another 46% in groups of two to three.

That has two consequences. A team rewarded for leads will generate several per opportunity and count each one. And a team that sees three people from one company each download one asset will score them as three weak leads, when Forrester's point is that this is a stronger signal than one person downloading three. McKinsey's 2024 B2B Pulse survey of nearly 4,000 decision makers found buyers use about ten interaction channels during a purchase, double the 2016 figure, which makes any single-touch lead count even less representative.

The fix is to move the unit of account up one level, to the qualified opportunity: a buying group with a confirmed need, a budget holder in contact and a dated next step. Our explainer on the marketing funnel covers how stages are usually drawn; the point here is that the economics should be calculated at the opportunity stage, because that is the first point at which sales and marketing agree something real exists.

The chain from spend to cash

The chain that matters has five links: spend, qualified opportunities, win rate, contract value after gross margin, and payback. ChartMogul's definition of the last link is standard: CAC payback in months equals customer acquisition cost divided by monthly revenue per account multiplied by gross margin. Gross margin belongs in the denominator because only the margin left after delivery costs can repay what was spent to win the customer.

A worked quarter shows how the links combine.

LinkIllustrative figureHow it is calculated
Programme spend£60,000Media, events, content and tools for the quarter
Qualified opportunities40Opportunities meeting the written definition
Cost per qualified opportunity£1,500£60,000 ÷ 40
Win rate25%Won ÷ qualified, for this cohort
New customers1040 × 25%
Sales cost for the quarter£90,000Salaries, commission and tools, allocated
Customer acquisition cost£15,000(£60,000 + £90,000) ÷ 10
Annual contract value£30,000Average for won deals
Monthly gross margin per customer£1,750£30,000 ÷ 12 × 70% margin
CAC payback8.6 months£15,000 ÷ £1,750

All figures are illustrative. The structure is what matters: a change in any one link moves payback, and the marketing team controls two of them directly (spend and the number of qualified opportunities) and influences a third (win rate, through the quality of what it sends).

Working backwards to a ceiling

The same chain run in reverse gives each channel a spending limit. Suppose the board has agreed a payback target of 12 months. Then:

  1. Maximum acquisition cost is 12 × £1,750 = £21,000 per customer.
  2. Subtract sales cost per win. At £90,000 a quarter and ten wins, that is £9,000, leaving £12,000 for marketing.
  3. Multiply by win rate. At 25%, the maximum marketing cost per qualified opportunity is £12,000 × 25% = £3,000.

Any channel producing qualified opportunities below £3,000 is inside the target; any channel above it is either subsidised by cheaper channels or losing money. The ceiling moves with win rate, which is why a segment where the firm wins one deal in eight can afford far less marketing per opportunity than one where it wins one in three. That is the economic case for the segment choices in Part 3.

A payback target is a budget rule in disguise. Work it backwards and every channel gets a price it must beat.

Two cautions. The ceiling uses average sales cost, and the marginal cost of the next opportunity is usually higher than the average, because the cheapest sources are used first. And win rate must be measured on the cohort of opportunities a channel produced, not on the firm's overall rate, or a channel that sends weak opportunities will borrow the credibility of the strong ones.

What the benchmarks say, and what they hide

Benchmarks are useful for orientation and dangerous as targets. Bessemer's analysis of its cloud portfolio found average CAC payback of about 15 months for companies with $1m to $10m of annual recurring revenue, and suggested targets of under 12 months for small-business customers, under 18 for mid-market and under 24 for enterprise. ChartMogul gives similar ranges, noting that sales cycle length and churn both affect whether a given payback is healthy.

Payback on its own hides retention. The 2025 SaaS Benchmarks report from Growth Unhinged and High Alpha, drawn from more than 800 companies, grouped respondents by payback and net revenue retention. Companies with low payback and high retention averaged 71% growth; those with high payback and low retention averaged 10%. A firm can hit its payback target by acquiring customers cheaply who leave quickly, and the payback figure will not show it. Report payback beside gross retention, as Part 7 recommends.

Benchmarks also come from recurring-revenue software firms. A services firm with project revenue has no monthly recurring margin to divide by. The equivalent is gross margin from the first year of work per client, and the same arithmetic applies.

Capture and creation

The hardest problem in demand economics is that the two kinds of spend behave differently and are measured as if they were the same.

6sense's 2024 Buyer Experience Report found buyers are nearly 70% of the way through their purchasing process before they contact a seller, and 81% already have a preferred vendor at first contact. Most of the decision is made before any lead form is filled in. Spend that reaches buyers in that period creates demand. Spend that catches them when they finally search for a vendor captures it.

Demand captureDemand creation
ExamplesBrand search, retargeting, review sites, inbound follow-upResearch, events, partner programmes, thought leadership, outbound to new segments
Time to effectDays to weeksMonths to quarters
How it looks in attributionCheap, because it sits next to the conversionExpensive, because credit is diluted or lost
What it actually tells youHow efficiently existing demand is harvestedWhether the pool of future buyers is growing
The usual errorOver-funding it because the cost per opportunity looks lowCutting it because the cost per opportunity looks high

Capture channels always look efficient because they sit closest to the conversion. Our piece on attribution versus incrementality covers how to estimate what they actually cause, including converting an incrementality share into a cost per caused outcome. The economic consequence is simple: apply the cost-per-opportunity ceiling to capture channels on an incremental basis, and judge creation channels on a longer window with a leading indicator agreed in advance, such as qualified opportunities from target accounts that had no prior contact.

Our explainer on brand versus performance marketing covers the wider argument. For budget purposes, the practical rule is to set the split deliberately, record it, and review it annually rather than letting the quarterly cost-per-opportunity report shift money towards capture one quarter at a time.

Velocity is part of the cost

The economics also depend on how fast opportunities turn into cash. Pipedrive's version of the standard sales velocity formula multiplies the number of opportunities by average deal size and win rate, and divides by sales cycle length. Shortening the cycle raises velocity without any change in spend.

That matters for demand budgets because cycle length sets how much pipeline is needed. As Part 7 noted, coverage requirements fall as cycles shorten. A firm that cuts its average cycle from 90 to 60 days needs roughly a third less pipeline in flight to land the same bookings in a year, which means a third less demand spend at the same cost per opportunity. Work that removes friction from the sales process is, in economic terms, demand generation.

Making the budget a recorded decision

The budget itself should be recorded as a decision, in the format The Build Order uses for any commercial decision worth recording: the allocation by channel, the reason, the owner, the expected cost per qualified opportunity for each channel, and a check date. At the check date, the actual cost per opportunity and the cohort win rate are written back.

After two or three quarters the record answers questions that a dashboard cannot: which channel forecasts were consistently optimistic, which channels improved with more spend and which degraded, and whether the creation budget produced the leading indicator it was meant to. Our piece on single-channel dependency covers the related risk of a budget that has drifted into one source.

Where the method strains. Long enterprise cycles mean a quarter's cohort may not close for a year; use stage progression as a leading indicator and say so. Small volumes mean a channel producing six opportunities a quarter will show noisy win rates; pool two or three quarters before acting. And opportunity definitions must be stable, or the cost per opportunity improves simply because the bar was lowered.

Illustrative example: the ceiling meets the events budget
Decision
Set a maximum cost per qualified opportunity of £3,000 for all capture channels, measured on incremental opportunities, and fund events on a two-quarter window against target-account opportunities.
Reason and owner
Events had been cut twice because their cost per lead looked high, while brand search absorbed the savings. Owned by the head of marketing; ceiling agreed with the finance director from the 12-month payback target.
What changed
Two paid search campaigns fell above the ceiling once measured incrementally and were cut; the events budget was restored for two quarters with a written check date.

Illustrative: a composite of a mid-size B2B technology firm, built from patterns across engagements; figures are illustrative.

lowob takeaways

  • Count opportunities, not leads. The qualified opportunity is the first unit sales and marketing both believe in.
  • Run the chain both ways. Forward it gives payback; backward it gives every channel a cost ceiling.
  • Read payback with retention. Cheap customers who leave are not efficient acquisition.
  • Measure capture incrementally. Channels next to the conversion always look cheaper than they are.
  • Record the budget. Expected cost per opportunity by channel, written back at a check date.
Gateway card

Before you set next quarter's demand budget

  • A written definition of a qualified opportunity, agreed by sales and marketing
  • Cost per qualified opportunity by channel for the last two quarters
  • Win rate by channel cohort, not the firm-wide average
  • A payback target agreed with finance, and the ceiling it implies
  • The split between capture and creation stated and recorded
  • A check date for each channel's expected cost per opportunity

Common questions

How do you calculate CAC payback?

Divide customer acquisition cost by the monthly revenue per account multiplied by gross margin. A £15,000 acquisition cost against £1,750 of monthly gross margin pays back in about 8.6 months.

What is a good CAC payback period for B2B?

Bessemer suggests under 12 months for small-business customers, under 18 for mid-market and under 24 for enterprise. Read it alongside retention, because cheap customers who churn can produce a good payback figure.

Why should marketing stop reporting leads?

Forrester finds fewer than 1% of leads become closed deals and several leads often feed one opportunity, so lead volume rewards activity rather than revenue. Qualified opportunities are a better unit.

How much should we spend per opportunity?

Work backwards from a payback target: maximum acquisition cost, minus sales cost per win, multiplied by win rate, gives the most marketing can spend per qualified opportunity.
